alignment_log.scope: Initial alignment pass: CDE T-SEL, CASEL, CA CTE (ICT) anchor standards.
alignment_log.note: Primary source was the teacher's own "One Word Lesson Plan" Google Doc (Aug 2025, linked from the post), which already maps the activity to T-SEL and CTE ICT anchors in detail. That doc is an administrative justification document (it cites nearly every competency area and anchor standard in reach, plus K-5 and 9-12 "if you taught it there" extensions this post never claims); this carrier is deliberately narrower -- only the specific codes the actual 6th-grade activity (five words, elimination, word-wall art, journal reflection) does on its own, not everything an ICT instructor could plausibly justify. RULER and VIA were checked and skipped: RULER is specifically about emotion vocabulary and regulation, which this activity doesn't teach (it's about identity, not feelings-in-the-moment), and VIA's character-strengths taxonomy doesn't map cleanly onto an identity-naming exercise without forcing it. No CS-content frameworks checked -- this lesson is explicitly orthogonal to the program's CS standards, same framing as the catalogs' own SEL group.

locator_titles.one-word-wall: Words That Built Our Classroom Community

meta.caveat: A single blog post, not a chaptered source -- locator_kind is "none". This is the first post in the porttack.com SEL category carrier; more SEL-tagged lesson plans will add their own locators here rather than new carrier files.

1.ID.note: The lesson's whole arc -- five words, then narrowing by elimination, to one -- is naming your own identity in the plainest sense this competency describes, right down to the standard's own "naming a feeling, naming what matters to you" framing matching the brainstorm categories (personality, hobbies, background/culture, goals, talents, values).

1.AG.note: The teacher's doc names "Demonstrating Self-Efficacy" explicitly (recognizing personal strengths and talents while choosing words); it's a real but secondary thread under the identity-naming activity, not the main point.

3.BE.note: The word wall itself is the belonging payoff: students see classmates' chosen words, ask questions, admire designs, and the collected wall becomes (in the post's own words) "our portrait." That's this standard's "being a good community member" framing made literal.

4.BE.note: The art-making phase doubles as unstructured peer interaction (helping with supplies, asking about word choices), a lighter-weight version of this standard's friendship/listening focus than 3.BE above.

SA.1.note: The word list itself blends personal traits (funny, determined, artistic) with social/cultural identities (italian, mexican, polish, american, christian, sister, brother) in the same brainstorm -- this competency's own definition, not an inference.

SOC.3.note: Reading and reacting to classmates' words during the art-making phase is a light touch of empathy/compassion, secondary to the identity work the lesson is actually built around.

3.1.note: The source doc (written from the teacher's CTE-instructor role) frames the self-reflection as career-readiness groundwork -- knowing your own interests, aptitudes, and traits. Honest caveat: that's the doc's own career-pathway framing applied to a 6th-grade icebreaker, not something the lesson teaches on its own terms; keep this one at partial rather than strong.

9.6.note: "Respect individual and cultural differences" is a workplace-diversity standard; the word wall's display of classmates' varied cultural/personal identities is a middle-school-scale analog of it, not a direct instance.

8.4.note: The lesson's own "safe space" rule -- share only what you're comfortable with, use a private code word if needed, never comment on someone else's choice -- is a real, age-appropriate version of this standard's confidentiality/personal-integrity concern, even though the standard itself is written for a workplace.
